critic_reason: Violates owner's swap-free/no interest-bearing instrument condition (requires short selling and leverage).
data_source: National central bank FX intervention bulletins (e.g., BIS, central bank websites) paired with daily EM FX spot rates.
evidence: Dominguez (1998), Journal of International Money and Finance, measured central bank intervention effects on exchange rates; this lab has not tested intervention-day follow-through in EM FX daily.
mechanism: Emerging-market central banks intervene to lean against currency moves for price stability, not profit. They are willing to lose money on intervention and have deeper pockets than speculators. Their order flow shifts the equilibrium rate for several days as the market absorbs the signal; speculators who fade intervention lose because the central bank’s objective is non-economic and persistent. The effect survives because intervention is discretionary, politically sensitive, and data arrives with a lag, limiting arbitrage.
needs_short_or_leverage: Yes: short selling and leverage (EM FX CFD).
rule: Each day, using central-bank net intervention data (USD vs the EM currency) released with a one-day lag, compute the intervention surprise as today’s intervention minus the 90-day rolling mean. If the surprise exceeds +2 standard deviations (central bank sold USD/bought EM currency), buy the EM currency/USD pair at the next day’s open; if below -2 SD (central bank bought USD/sold EM currency), sell the pair at the next day’s open. Hold exactly 5 trading days and exit at the close. No position otherwise. Sizing is fixed at one unit; no look-ahead because the intervention figure is known before the next open.
title: EM FX central bank intervention follow-through
why: Violates owner's swap-free/no interest-bearing instrument condition (requires short selling and leverage).
why_new: New mechanism (non-profit central bank order flow), new data (intervention day flags), and new market for this lab (em-fx-daily has only one prior test, none on intervention).

critic_reason: Violates owner's swap-free/no interest-bearing instrument condition (requires short selling and leverage).
data_source: U.S. Energy Information Administration Weekly Petroleum Status Report (crude oil inventories) and crude oil futures/CFD intraday bars.
evidence: none: a new idea (EIA crude surprise same-day mean reversion not in the tested list; natural-gas storage drift was tested, not crude inventory mean reversion).
mechanism: The EIA Weekly Petroleum Status Report moves crude oil on the headline inventory number. Algorithmic and retail participants overreact to the surprise while ignoring offsetting details (refinery runs, imports, SPR releases). The price overshoots and reverts over the same session as liquidity providers absorb the flow. Momentum chasers lose; the effect persists because the release is scheduled, the overreaction is behavioral, and arbitrage capital is limited by the speed and risk of the initial move.
needs_short_or_leverage: Yes: short selling and leverage (energy CFD).
rule: Every Wednesday at the EIA 10:30 ET release, compute the crude inventory surprise as today’s change minus the prior 4-week average change. If the surprise is above +1.5 standard deviations of the prior 52-week surprise distribution, sell one unit of crude at 10:45 ET and buy to cover at 16:00 ET the same day. If below -1.5 SD, buy at 10:45 ET and sell at 16:00 ET. No position otherwise. The prior 4-week average is known before the release, so there is no look-ahead.
title: EIA crude oil inventory surprise same-day mean reversion
why: Violates owner's swap-free/no interest-bearing instrument condition (requires short selling and leverage).
why_new: New mechanism (headline overreaction at scheduled EIA crude release), new data (crude inventory surprise series), and energy-futures-eia has only one prior test on a different topic (natural gas storage drift).

critic_reason: Meets all rejection criteria; mechanism is economic, data available, no condition breach.
data_source: World Gold Council Gold Demand Trends (central bank purchases by month) and daily gold futures prices.
evidence: none: a new idea (central-bank gold purchase timing is not in the tested list; gold trend, autumn, overnight, and Asian-hour rules were tested, but not central-bank flow timing).
mechanism: Central banks buy gold monthly for reserve diversification and de-dollarization. They are price-insensitive, long-term buyers with no profit motive and no stop-loss. Their purchases create persistent demand that the market underreacts to because gold is usually priced through real-rate and yield lenses. Speculators fighting the flow lose; the effect persists because central bank reserve accumulation is structural, multi-year, and not arbitraged away by profit-driven traders.
needs_short_or_leverage: No short selling; no leverage required (1x gold CFD possible).
rule: At the close on the first trading day after the World Gold Council monthly Gold Demand Trends report, if net central bank gold purchases in the reported month exceed the trailing 12-month average, buy one unit of gold at the next day’s open and hold until the close on the first trading day after the next report; then reassess. If purchases do not exceed the average, remain flat. No look-ahead: the report is public before the next day’s open. One round trip per month, so spread/slippage are a small fraction of the monthly move.
title: Central bank gold purchase follow-through
